I lost my train of thought in front of 31 seventh graders and I just stood there.

Dead silent. Chalk in my hand. Mouth half open.

I knew I'd been saying something about the Louisiana Purchase. I knew there was a next word coming. And then there just wasn't. It was like reaching for a light switch in a room you've walked into ten thousand times and finding nothing but flat wall.

The kids noticed. Of course they noticed. Kids notice everything. A boy in the second row, sweet kid, said "Mrs. Dunmore? You okay?" and I said yes, fine, sorry, lost my place, and I looked back down at my notes and pretended to find it.

But I hadn't lost my place.

My feet were buzzing. Both of them, that pins and needles feeling like when your foot falls asleep, except it wasn't going away, and there was this fog sitting over everything in my head like somebody had run a low cloud through the classroom.

And I remember thinking, very clearly, in the one part of my brain that was still working right: this is the thing. This is the thing that's going to take it all from me.

Let me back up and tell you who I am.

My name is Diane. I'm 56 years old and I live in Pueblo, Colorado, where I've taught, or substituted, or coached, or done lunch duty, in just about every school in the district at one point or another over 28 years. I had my own classroom for most of it. Eighth grade history. Then about six years ago, after my husband's heart scare, I went part time and started subbing so we'd have more flexibility, and I never really went back to full time.

I'm a widow now. Frank passed in 2022. So the subbing became the thing that got me out of the house, the thing that kept me feeling like myself. A school calls at 6:15 in the morning, I'm up and dressed and out the door by 7, and for the day I'm not a widow rattling around an empty house, I'm Mrs. Dunmore and somebody needs me.

That mattered more than I can tell you. The classroom was the last room in my life where I knew exactly who I was.

Which is why what was happening to me was so frightening.

It had started in my feet maybe two years before that day with the Louisiana Purchase. A tingling. A numbness in my toes that I figured was my shoes, then figured was my circulation, then figured was just one of those things that happens when you get to be my age and you've been on your feet in front of a chalkboard for three decades.

That's what my doctor figured too. "You're 54, Diane, you've been standing on hard floors your whole career. Some nerve stuff is normal." He told me to wear better shoes. I bought better shoes.

The tingling kept coming. Then it started at night, this burning along the bottoms of my feet that would wake me up at 2 in the morning, and I'd lie there in the dark on Frank's side of the bed because I'd started sleeping on his side after he passed, and I'd just wait for it to ease off enough to sleep again.

And the fog. The fog was the part I didn't tell anybody about, because how do you even describe it. It wasn't forgetting where my keys were. Everybody does that. It was standing in front of a sentence I'd said a thousand times and watching the end of it walk away from me. It was reading a paragraph and getting to the bottom and realizing I'd have to read it again because nothing stuck.

For a substitute teacher, that's not an inconvenience. That's the job leaving you.

I started keeping more notes. Bigger notes. I'd write out almost word for word what I was going to say, which I'd never needed to do in my life, because I was the woman who could teach the entire causes of the Civil War with no notes and a cup of coffee. Now I needed a script just to get through a worksheet day.

I told myself it was grief. People say grief does things to your brain, and Lord knows I had the grief for it. I told myself it was age. I told myself it was the floors, the shoes, the standing.

I told myself a lot of things, because the alternative, the thing I was actually scared of, was that something was wrong with me. Wrong in a way that doesn't get better. Wrong in a way that was going to keep eating little pieces off the edges of who I was until there wasn't a Mrs. Dunmore left to call at 6:15 in the morning.

That day with the seventh graders, I drove home and I sat in my car in the driveway and I cried in a way I hadn't cried since the funeral.

Because I'd finally said the scary thing out loud to myself. I am losing it. Whatever it is, it's winning, and nobody can tell me why, and I'm going to end up one of those people who can't be left in charge of a classroom or a checkbook or a stove.

That's where I was. I want you to know exactly how low that was, because what happened next only matters if you understand the hole I was in.

What happened next was my sister-in-law, Rosa.

Rosa was married to Frank's brother. After Frank died we stayed close, two women who'd married into the same family and outlived the men. She'd come over on Sundays. And one Sunday in the spring she's sitting at my kitchen table and I'm trying to tell her a story and I lose the word again, right in front of her, the word just gone, and I see her watching me.

And she doesn't say "are you okay" the way the kids did. She says, very quietly, "Diane. How long has that been happening?"

And I don't know why, but I told her. All of it. The feet. The burning at night. The fog. The notes I had to write now. The day I went silent in front of 31 children. I told her the scary thing, that I thought I was losing my mind, and I cried again right there at the table.

Rosa let me finish. And then she said something I wasn't expecting.

She said, "My cousin Teresa had the feet thing. The burning. The numb toes. Hers got bad, she was dropping things, couldn't feel the gas pedal right. And the fog too, she used to call it walking around in pudding."

I said, what happened to her.

And Rosa said, "She's better. She's a lot better. And it wasn't a drug. It was a little berry thing she found. I'll text her, you should talk to her."

Now I want to be honest about where my head went, because I think it's the same place yours would go.

A berry. I'm a history teacher. I deal in evidence. I have spent my whole life teaching kids the difference between what's true and what somebody wishes were true. And here's Rosa telling me her cousin fixed her numb feet and her foggy head with a piece of fruit.

I didn't believe it. Not for a second. I thought, that poor woman probably got better on her own and gave the credit to a vitamin, and now Rosa's going to have me chasing some online nonsense while my brain rots.

But I was also desperate. And desperate and skeptical can live in the same person at the same time, I've learned. So when Teresa called me that week, I picked up. And I figured I'd hear her out and then go back to being scared.

Teresa didn't try to sell me anything. That's the first thing that got me. She just told me her story, which sounded so much like mine I got goosebumps, and then she explained how the thing actually worked. And it was the explanation that turned me, not the testimonial. Because for the first time, somebody connected my feet and my fog into one single thing, and once she did, I couldn't unsee it.

Here's what she told me.

She said, think about what your nerves actually are. They're cells. And cells need energy to do their job, the same way your car needs gas. The energy in your cells gets made by these tiny little engines inside them called mitochondria. Every cell's got them. They're the power plant.

And here's the part I never knew.

Nerve cells, Teresa said, are some of the hungriest cells in your entire body. They burn through more energy than almost anything else you've got, because they're firing signals constantly, maintaining their coating, keeping the lines open. They run hot. They need a lot of fuel.

So when the power plants start running down, when your mitochondria aren't making energy the way they used to because of age and stress and processed food and all the wear of a long life, guess which cells feel it first?

The hungriest ones. The nerves.

And I just sat there on the phone in my kitchen with my hand over my mouth.

Because she'd just explained my feet and my fog in one breath. The nerves in my feet, starved for energy, sending up that tingling and burning to say something's wrong down here. And the nerves in my brain, also starved, also among the hungriest cells I've got, sitting there in the fog because they didn't have the fuel to fire clean and quick the way they used to.

Same problem. Two ends of the same body. One cause.

And every single thing my doctor had told me suddenly made sense as a thing that wouldn't work. Better shoes don't feed a starving cell. There was no pill anybody offered me, but Teresa said even the stuff people take for the burning, it just quiets the signal, it doesn't do a thing about why the signal's there. It's like the engine light's on in your car and somebody puts a piece of tape over the light. You can't see it anymore. The engine's still starving.

Nobody was feeding the power plants. That was the whole thing. That was the hole in everything I'd tried.

So then I asked the obvious question. Okay. How does a berry feed a power plant?

And this is where she told me about amla.

Amla's an Indian gooseberry. People over there have eaten it for thousands of years, which, the history teacher in me appreciated, because I trust an old thing that's lasted longer than I trust a new thing that's loud.

And inside amla there's a thing it does, it helps switch on something in your body called AMPK. Teresa called it the body's energy switch. And when that switch is on, it tells your mitochondria, your power plants, to get back to work and make energy more efficiently, closer to the way they did when you were younger.

So the fuel starts flowing again. Back into your cells.

And because your nerve cells are the hungriest, the ones that felt the shortage first, they can be among the first to feel it when the fuel comes back. When those nerve cells are better supported, they can get back to the work of keeping up their protective coating and carrying their signals clean, and that burning, that buzzing, it can start to settle down so the feeling comes back instead of the noise.

Teresa also said amla's got one of the highest antioxidant loads of any food anybody's ever measured, and that part matters because antioxidants help protect those little power plants from the wear that ran them down in the first place. So you're not just refueling. You're protecting.

She told me the brand she used. Auniva. Their Amla. Two little capsules a day, made right here in the USA, and she'd been taking it for the better part of a year.

I'm going to tell you the truth about what I did next, which is I argued with myself for two more days.

The skeptic in me said: Diane, you fall for this, you're exactly the kind of person you warn your students about. The desperate widow buying magic beans.

But the other part of me, the part that had stood silent in front of 31 children, said: you have tried being a skeptic about your own feet for two years and being a skeptic hasn't given you a single night of sleep back.

And then there was the thing Teresa mentioned almost in passing. She said Auniva gives you 90 days. Take it, see what happens, and if nothing does, you send it back and they refund you. The whole thing.

And that was what tipped it. Because a skeptic's whole worry is getting taken. Getting fooled. Spending money on nothing. And here was a thing telling me, try it for three months, watch your own body, and if I was right to be skeptical, I lose nothing but the wondering.

The skeptic didn't have an argument for that. So I ordered it.

Now here's the honest account of what happened, and I'm telling it careful because I was a careful person about this the whole way through, watching myself like I'd watch a kid I suspected was exaggerating.

The first two weeks, nothing. I'll be straight with you. I almost decided it was the nonsense I'd feared.

Around week three, the nights changed first. I wasn't waking up at 2 with my feet on fire as much. I noticed because I started sleeping until the alarm, and I hadn't done that in a long, long time. I figured it was a fluke. It kept happening.

By the end of the first month the buzzing in my feet during the day had backed off. Not gone. But quieter. I'd be standing at a chalkboard and realize I wasn't thinking about my feet, which, if you've had it, you know how loud that quiet is.

And the fog. This is the one I almost can't talk about without getting emotional. Somewhere in the second month I was teaching, an actual lesson, off the top of my head, and I got to the end of a long explanation and realized I hadn't reached for a single note. The sentence had a beginning and a middle and an end and I'd walked the whole length of it without the floor dropping out.

I had to turn around and face the chalkboard for a second so the kids wouldn't see my face.

By month three I'd stopped writing out the word for word scripts. I went back to a cup of coffee and a couple bullet points, the way I'd taught my whole life. A school called me at 6:15 one morning for a long term assignment, six weeks covering a maternity leave, eighth grade history, my old subject, and I said yes without the fear that used to come with yes.

I want to be careful about what I'm claiming here, because I respect you too much to oversell it. I'm not telling you a berry rebuilt my brain. I'm telling you that the thing I'd been losing, the feeling in my feet and the sharpness in my head and the simple confidence to stand in front of a room and be myself, came back enough that I'm a working teacher again instead of a scared woman in a driveway.

That's the felt truth of it. That's what I've got.

I called Rosa and I cried again, but a different kind that time. And then I called Teresa, and I think I embarrassed her with how much I thanked her.

So here's why I'm sitting here typing this out instead of just keeping it to myself.

Because I know there's a version of you reading this who's got the buzzing in the feet. Or the fog you haven't told anybody about because you're scared of what it means. Or both, and you haven't connected them, because nobody's told you they're two ends of the same starving thing.

And I know somebody's told you it's just your age. Just your shoes. Just stress. Just one of those things.

I heard all of that. For two years. And all it did was let it get worse while I waited.

I'm not telling you to skip your doctor. Go. Keep going. I went. But I am telling you that there's a part of this nobody walked me through until a stranger on the phone did, and it's the part that finally explained why nothing I'd tried touched it. The power plants. The fuel. The hungry nerves at the end of the line.

Auniva's Amla is what helped me feed them. A little berry people have trusted for thousands of years, two capsules a day, made right here.

And you get the 90 days. That's the part I keep coming back to, because it's the part that let a lifelong skeptic finally just try. You take it, you watch your own body the way I watched mine, and if I'm wrong and it does nothing for you, you send it back and you get every dollar back. The only thing you're risking is staying right where you are, waiting, the way I waited.

I almost lost the last room in my life where I knew who I was.

I'm standing in it again Monday morning. Eighth grade history. No script. Just coffee.

If you've been standing silent in your own version of that classroom, wondering if it's all slipping away, maybe go find out why before you let anybody tell you it's just your age.

👉 auniva.co/amla/33

P.S. The long term assignment turned into them asking me to come back full time in the fall. I said I'd think about it. Two years ago I couldn't get through a worksheet. I keep that fact close, because it reminds me how fast scared can turn into something else.

P.P.S. I want to say one more time, plain, that the 90 day guarantee is the only reason I got over myself and ordered. If you're a skeptic like me, hold onto that. You are not being asked to believe anything. You're being asked to try it and watch, and they'll give your money back if you're right to doubt it. That's a fair deal for a careful person. It was fair enough for me. 👉 auniva.co/amla/33

P.P.P.S. Rosa still comes over on Sundays. Last week I told her a whole long story start to finish and never lost the thread once, and she just smiled at me over her coffee and didn't say a word, because she didn't have to. 👉 auniva.co/amla/33

That obsession turned into Acu Seeds, which is now East Healing - and somewhere along the way I ended up on Dragons’ Den and have helped 125,000 customers.

Ear seeds are small but they’re quietly doing a lot. The results people share with us still stop me in my tracks.

It’s been a wild ride and honestly, we’re just getting started.

more","cards":[],"body":{"text":"I lost my train of thought in front of 31 seventh graders and I just stood there.

Dead silent. Chalk in my hand. Mouth half open.

I knew I'd been saying something about the Louisiana Purchase. I knew there was a next word coming. And then there just wasn't. It was like reaching for a light switch in a room you've walked into ten thousand times and finding nothing but flat wall.

The kids noticed. Of course they noticed. Kids notice everything. A boy in the second row, sweet kid, said "Mrs. Dunmore? You okay?" and I said yes, fine, sorry, lost my place, and I looked back down at my notes and pretended to find it.

But I hadn't lost my place.

My feet were buzzing. Both of them, that pins and needles feeling like when your foot falls asleep, except it wasn't going away, and there was this fog sitting over everything in my head like somebody had run a low cloud through the classroom.

And I remember thinking, very clearly, in the one part of my brain that was still working right: this is the thing. This is the thing that's going to take it all from me.

Let me back up and tell you who I am.

My name is Diane. I'm 56 years old and I live in Pueblo, Colorado, where I've taught, or substituted, or coached, or done lunch duty, in just about every school in the district at one point or another over 28 years. I had my own classroom for most of it. Eighth grade history. Then about six years ago, after my husband's heart scare, I went part time and started subbing so we'd have more flexibility, and I never really went back to full time.

I'm a widow now. Frank passed in 2022. So the subbing became the thing that got me out of the house, the thing that kept me feeling like myself. A school calls at 6:15 in the morning, I'm up and dressed and out the door by 7, and for the day I'm not a widow rattling around an empty house, I'm Mrs. Dunmore and somebody needs me.

That mattered more than I can tell you. The classroom was the last room in my life where I knew exactly who I was.

Which is why what was happening to me was so frightening.

It had started in my feet maybe two years before that day with the Louisiana Purchase. A tingling. A numbness in my toes that I figured was my shoes, then figured was my circulation, then figured was just one of those things that happens when you get to be my age and you've been on your feet in front of a chalkboard for three decades.

That's what my doctor figured too. "You're 54, Diane, you've been standing on hard floors your whole career. Some nerve stuff is normal." He told me to wear better shoes. I bought better shoes.

The tingling kept coming. Then it started at night, this burning along the bottoms of my feet that would wake me up at 2 in the morning, and I'd lie there in the dark on Frank's side of the bed because I'd started sleeping on his side after he passed, and I'd just wait for it to ease off enough to sleep again.

And the fog. The fog was the part I didn't tell anybody about, because how do you even describe it. It wasn't forgetting where my keys were. Everybody does that. It was standing in front of a sentence I'd said a thousand times and watching the end of it walk away from me. It was reading a paragraph and getting to the bottom and realizing I'd have to read it again because nothing stuck.

For a substitute teacher, that's not an inconvenience. That's the job leaving you.

I started keeping more notes. Bigger notes. I'd write out almost word for word what I was going to say, which I'd never needed to do in my life, because I was the woman who could teach the entire causes of the Civil War with no notes and a cup of coffee. Now I needed a script just to get through a worksheet day.

I told myself it was grief. People say grief does things to your brain, and Lord knows I had the grief for it. I told myself it was age. I told myself it was the floors, the shoes, the standing.

I told myself a lot of things, because the alternative, the thing I was actually scared of, was that something was wrong with me. Wrong in a way that doesn't get better. Wrong in a way that was going to keep eating little pieces off the edges of who I was until there wasn't a Mrs. Dunmore left to call at 6:15 in the morning.

That day with the seventh graders, I drove home and I sat in my car in the driveway and I cried in a way I hadn't cried since the funeral.

Because I'd finally said the scary thing out loud to myself. I am losing it. Whatever it is, it's winning, and nobody can tell me why, and I'm going to end up one of those people who can't be left in charge of a classroom or a checkbook or a stove.

That's where I was. I want you to know exactly how low that was, because what happened next only matters if you understand the hole I was in.

What happened next was my sister-in-law, Rosa.

Rosa was married to Frank's brother. After Frank died we stayed close, two women who'd married into the same family and outlived the men. She'd come over on Sundays. And one Sunday in the spring she's sitting at my kitchen table and I'm trying to tell her a story and I lose the word again, right in front of her, the word just gone, and I see her watching me.

And she doesn't say "are you okay" the way the kids did. She says, very quietly, "Diane. How long has that been happening?"

And I don't know why, but I told her. All of it. The feet. The burning at night. The fog. The notes I had to write now. The day I went silent in front of 31 children. I told her the scary thing, that I thought I was losing my mind, and I cried again right there at the table.

Rosa let me finish. And then she said something I wasn't expecting.

She said, "My cousin Teresa had the feet thing. The burning. The numb toes. Hers got bad, she was dropping things, couldn't feel the gas pedal right. And the fog too, she used to call it walking around in pudding."

I said, what happened to her.

And Rosa said, "She's better. She's a lot better. And it wasn't a drug. It was a little berry thing she found. I'll text her, you should talk to her."

Now I want to be honest about where my head went, because I think it's the same place yours would go.

A berry. I'm a history teacher. I deal in evidence. I have spent my whole life teaching kids the difference between what's true and what somebody wishes were true. And here's Rosa telling me her cousin fixed her numb feet and her foggy head with a piece of fruit.

I didn't believe it. Not for a second. I thought, that poor woman probably got better on her own and gave the credit to a vitamin, and now Rosa's going to have me chasing some online nonsense while my brain rots.

But I was also desperate. And desperate and skeptical can live in the same person at the same time, I've learned. So when Teresa called me that week, I picked up. And I figured I'd hear her out and then go back to being scared.

Teresa didn't try to sell me anything. That's the first thing that got me. She just told me her story, which sounded so much like mine I got goosebumps, and then she explained how the thing actually worked. And it was the explanation that turned me, not the testimonial. Because for the first time, somebody connected my feet and my fog into one single thing, and once she did, I couldn't unsee it.

Here's what she told me.

She said, think about what your nerves actually are. They're cells. And cells need energy to do their job, the same way your car needs gas. The energy in your cells gets made by these tiny little engines inside them called mitochondria. Every cell's got them. They're the power plant.

And here's the part I never knew.

Nerve cells, Teresa said, are some of the hungriest cells in your entire body. They burn through more energy than almost anything else you've got, because they're firing signals constantly, maintaining their coating, keeping the lines open. They run hot. They need a lot of fuel.

So when the power plants start running down, when your mitochondria aren't making energy the way they used to because of age and stress and processed food and all the wear of a long life, guess which cells feel it first?

The hungriest ones. The nerves.

And I just sat there on the phone in my kitchen with my hand over my mouth.

Because she'd just explained my feet and my fog in one breath. The nerves in my feet, starved for energy, sending up that tingling and burning to say something's wrong down here. And the nerves in my brain, also starved, also among the hungriest cells I've got, sitting there in the fog because they didn't have the fuel to fire clean and quick the way they used to.

Same problem. Two ends of the same body. One cause.

And every single thing my doctor had told me suddenly made sense as a thing that wouldn't work. Better shoes don't feed a starving cell. There was no pill anybody offered me, but Teresa said even the stuff people take for the burning, it just quiets the signal, it doesn't do a thing about why the signal's there. It's like the engine light's on in your car and somebody puts a piece of tape over the light. You can't see it anymore. The engine's still starving.

Nobody was feeding the power plants. That was the whole thing. That was the hole in everything I'd tried.

So then I asked the obvious question. Okay. How does a berry feed a power plant?

And this is where she told me about amla.

Amla's an Indian gooseberry. People over there have eaten it for thousands of years, which, the history teacher in me appreciated, because I trust an old thing that's lasted longer than I trust a new thing that's loud.

And inside amla there's a thing it does, it helps switch on something in your body called AMPK. Teresa called it the body's energy switch. And when that switch is on, it tells your mitochondria, your power plants, to get back to work and make energy more efficiently, closer to the way they did when you were younger.

So the fuel starts flowing again. Back into your cells.

And because your nerve cells are the hungriest, the ones that felt the shortage first, they can be among the first to feel it when the fuel comes back. When those nerve cells are better supported, they can get back to the work of keeping up their protective coating and carrying their signals clean, and that burning, that buzzing, it can start to settle down so the feeling comes back instead of the noise.

Teresa also said amla's got one of the highest antioxidant loads of any food anybody's ever measured, and that part matters because antioxidants help protect those little power plants from the wear that ran them down in the first place. So you're not just refueling. You're protecting.

She told me the brand she used. Auniva. Their Amla. Two little capsules a day, made right here in the USA, and she'd been taking it for the better part of a year.

I'm going to tell you the truth about what I did next, which is I argued with myself for two more days.

The skeptic in me said: Diane, you fall for this, you're exactly the kind of person you warn your students about. The desperate widow buying magic beans.

But the other part of me, the part that had stood silent in front of 31 children, said: you have tried being a skeptic about your own feet for two years and being a skeptic hasn't given you a single night of sleep back.

And then there was the thing Teresa mentioned almost in passing. She said Auniva gives you 90 days. Take it, see what happens, and if nothing does, you send it back and they refund you. The whole thing.

And that was what tipped it. Because a skeptic's whole worry is getting taken. Getting fooled. Spending money on nothing. And here was a thing telling me, try it for three months, watch your own body, and if I was right to be skeptical, I lose nothing but the wondering.

The skeptic didn't have an argument for that. So I ordered it.

Now here's the honest account of what happened, and I'm telling it careful because I was a careful person about this the whole way through, watching myself like I'd watch a kid I suspected was exaggerating.

The first two weeks, nothing. I'll be straight with you. I almost decided it was the nonsense I'd feared.

Around week three, the nights changed first. I wasn't waking up at 2 with my feet on fire as much. I noticed because I started sleeping until the alarm, and I hadn't done that in a long, long time. I figured it was a fluke. It kept happening.

By the end of the first month the buzzing in my feet during the day had backed off. Not gone. But quieter. I'd be standing at a chalkboard and realize I wasn't thinking about my feet, which, if you've had it, you know how loud that quiet is.

And the fog. This is the one I almost can't talk about without getting emotional. Somewhere in the second month I was teaching, an actual lesson, off the top of my head, and I got to the end of a long explanation and realized I hadn't reached for a single note. The sentence had a beginning and a middle and an end and I'd walked the whole length of it without the floor dropping out.

I had to turn around and face the chalkboard for a second so the kids wouldn't see my face.

By month three I'd stopped writing out the word for word scripts. I went back to a cup of coffee and a couple bullet points, the way I'd taught my whole life. A school called me at 6:15 one morning for a long term assignment, six weeks covering a maternity leave, eighth grade history, my old subject, and I said yes without the fear that used to come with yes.

I want to be careful about what I'm claiming here, because I respect you too much to oversell it. I'm not telling you a berry rebuilt my brain. I'm telling you that the thing I'd been losing, the feeling in my feet and the sharpness in my head and the simple confidence to stand in front of a room and be myself, came back enough that I'm a working teacher again instead of a scared woman in a driveway.

That's the felt truth of it. That's what I've got.

I called Rosa and I cried again, but a different kind that time. And then I called Teresa, and I think I embarrassed her with how much I thanked her.

So here's why I'm sitting here typing this out instead of just keeping it to myself.

Because I know there's a version of you reading this who's got the buzzing in the feet. Or the fog you haven't told anybody about because you're scared of what it means. Or both, and you haven't connected them, because nobody's told you they're two ends of the same starving thing.

And I know somebody's told you it's just your age. Just your shoes. Just stress. Just one of those things.

I heard all of that. For two years. And all it did was let it get worse while I waited.

I'm not telling you to skip your doctor. Go. Keep going. I went. But I am telling you that there's a part of this nobody walked me through until a stranger on the phone did, and it's the part that finally explained why nothing I'd tried touched it. The power plants. The fuel. The hungry nerves at the end of the line.

Auniva's Amla is what helped me feed them. A little berry people have trusted for thousands of years, two capsules a day, made right here.

And you get the 90 days. That's the part I keep coming back to, because it's the part that let a lifelong skeptic finally just try. You take it, you watch your own body the way I watched mine, and if I'm wrong and it does nothing for you, you send it back and you get every dollar back. The only thing you're risking is staying right where you are, waiting, the way I waited.

I almost lost the last room in my life where I knew who I was.

I'm standing in it again Monday morning. Eighth grade history. No script. Just coffee.

If you've been standing silent in your own version of that classroom, wondering if it's all slipping away, maybe go find out why before you let anybody tell you it's just your age.

Dead silent. Chalk in my hand. Mouth half open.

I knew I'd been saying something about the Louisiana Purchase. I knew there was a next word coming. And then there just wasn't. It was like reaching for a light switch in a room you've walked into ten thousand times and finding nothing but flat wall.

The kids noticed. Of course they noticed. Kids notice everything. A boy in the second row, sweet kid, said "Mrs. Dunmore? You okay?" and I said yes, fine, sorry, lost my place, and I looked back down at my notes and pretended to find it.

But I hadn't lost my place.

My feet were buzzing. Both of them, that pins and needles feeling like when your foot falls asleep, except it wasn't going away, and there was this fog sitting over everything in my head like somebody had run a low cloud through the classroom.

And I remember thinking, very clearly, in the one part of my brain that was still working right: this is the thing. This is the thing that's going to take it all from me.

Let me back up and tell you who I am.

My name is Diane. I'm 56 years old and I live in Pueblo, Colorado, where I've taught, or substituted, or coached, or done lunch duty, in just about every school in the district at one point or another over 28 years. I had my own classroom for most of it. Eighth grade history. Then about six years ago, after my husband's heart scare, I went part time and started subbing so we'd have more flexibility, and I never really went back to full time.

I'm a widow now. Frank passed in 2022. So the subbing became the thing that got me out of the house, the thing that kept me feeling like myself. A school calls at 6:15 in the morning, I'm up and dressed and out the door by 7, and for the day I'm not a widow rattling around an empty house, I'm Mrs. Dunmore and somebody needs me.

That mattered more than I can tell you. The classroom was the last room in my life where I knew exactly who I was.

Which is why what was happening to me was so frightening.

It had started in my feet maybe two years before that day with the Louisiana Purchase. A tingling. A numbness in my toes that I figured was my shoes, then figured was my circulation, then figured was just one of those things that happens when you get to be my age and you've been on your feet in front of a chalkboard for three decades.

That's what my doctor figured too. "You're 54, Diane, you've been standing on hard floors your whole career. Some nerve stuff is normal." He told me to wear better shoes. I bought better shoes.

The tingling kept coming. Then it started at night, this burning along the bottoms of my feet that would wake me up at 2 in the morning, and I'd lie there in the dark on Frank's side of the bed because I'd started sleeping on his side after he passed, and I'd just wait for it to ease off enough to sleep again.

And the fog. The fog was the part I didn't tell anybody about, because how do you even describe it. It wasn't forgetting where my keys were. Everybody does that. It was standing in front of a sentence I'd said a thousand times and watching the end of it walk away from me. It was reading a paragraph and getting to the bottom and realizing I'd have to read it again because nothing stuck.

For a substitute teacher, that's not an inconvenience. That's the job leaving you.

I started keeping more notes. Bigger notes. I'd write out almost word for word what I was going to say, which I'd never needed to do in my life, because I was the woman who could teach the entire causes of the Civil War with no notes and a cup of coffee. Now I needed a script just to get through a worksheet day.

I told myself it was grief. People say grief does things to your brain, and Lord knows I had the grief for it. I told myself it was age. I told myself it was the floors, the shoes, the standing.

I told myself a lot of things, because the alternative, the thing I was actually scared of, was that something was wrong with me. Wrong in a way that doesn't get better. Wrong in a way that was going to keep eating little pieces off the edges of who I was until there wasn't a Mrs. Dunmore left to call at 6:15 in the morning.

That day with the seventh graders, I drove home and I sat in my car in the driveway and I cried in a way I hadn't cried since the funeral.

Because I'd finally said the scary thing out loud to myself. I am losing it. Whatever it is, it's winning, and nobody can tell me why, and I'm going to end up one of those people who can't be left in charge of a classroom or a checkbook or a stove.

That's where I was. I want you to know exactly how low that was, because what happened next only matters if you understand the hole I was in.

What happened next was my sister-in-law, Rosa.

Rosa was married to Frank's brother. After Frank died we stayed close, two women who'd married into the same family and outlived the men. She'd come over on Sundays. And one Sunday in the spring she's sitting at my kitchen table and I'm trying to tell her a story and I lose the word again, right in front of her, the word just gone, and I see her watching me.

And she doesn't say "are you okay" the way the kids did. She says, very quietly, "Diane. How long has that been happening?"

And I don't know why, but I told her. All of it. The feet. The burning at night. The fog. The notes I had to write now. The day I went silent in front of 31 children. I told her the scary thing, that I thought I was losing my mind, and I cried again right there at the table.

Rosa let me finish. And then she said something I wasn't expecting.

She said, "My cousin Teresa had the feet thing. The burning. The numb toes. Hers got bad, she was dropping things, couldn't feel the gas pedal right. And the fog too, she used to call it walking around in pudding."

I said, what happened to her.

And Rosa said, "She's better. She's a lot better. And it wasn't a drug. It was a little berry thing she found. I'll text her, you should talk to her."

Now I want to be honest about where my head went, because I think it's the same place yours would go.

A berry. I'm a history teacher. I deal in evidence. I have spent my whole life teaching kids the difference between what's true and what somebody wishes were true. And here's Rosa telling me her cousin fixed her numb feet and her foggy head with a piece of fruit.

I didn't believe it. Not for a second. I thought, that poor woman probably got better on her own and gave the credit to a vitamin, and now Rosa's going to have me chasing some online nonsense while my brain rots.

But I was also desperate. And desperate and skeptical can live in the same person at the same time, I've learned. So when Teresa called me that week, I picked up. And I figured I'd hear her out and then go back to being scared.

Teresa didn't try to sell me anything. That's the first thing that got me. She just told me her story, which sounded so much like mine I got goosebumps, and then she explained how the thing actually worked. And it was the explanation that turned me, not the testimonial. Because for the first time, somebody connected my feet and my fog into one single thing, and once she did, I couldn't unsee it.

Here's what she told me.

She said, think about what your nerves actually are. They're cells. And cells need energy to do their job, the same way your car needs gas. The energy in your cells gets made by these tiny little engines inside them called mitochondria. Every cell's got them. They're the power plant.

And here's the part I never knew.

Nerve cells, Teresa said, are some of the hungriest cells in your entire body. They burn through more energy than almost anything else you've got, because they're firing signals constantly, maintaining their coating, keeping the lines open. They run hot. They need a lot of fuel.

So when the power plants start running down, when your mitochondria aren't making energy the way they used to because of age and stress and processed food and all the wear of a long life, guess which cells feel it first?

The hungriest ones. The nerves.

And I just sat there on the phone in my kitchen with my hand over my mouth.

Because she'd just explained my feet and my fog in one breath. The nerves in my feet, starved for energy, sending up that tingling and burning to say something's wrong down here. And the nerves in my brain, also starved, also among the hungriest cells I've got, sitting there in the fog because they didn't have the fuel to fire clean and quick the way they used to.

Same problem. Two ends of the same body. One cause.

And every single thing my doctor had told me suddenly made sense as a thing that wouldn't work. Better shoes don't feed a starving cell. There was no pill anybody offered me, but Teresa said even the stuff people take for the burning, it just quiets the signal, it doesn't do a thing about why the signal's there. It's like the engine light's on in your car and somebody puts a piece of tape over the light. You can't see it anymore. The engine's still starving.

Nobody was feeding the power plants. That was the whole thing. That was the hole in everything I'd tried.

So then I asked the obvious question. Okay. How does a berry feed a power plant?

And this is where she told me about amla.

Amla's an Indian gooseberry. People over there have eaten it for thousands of years, which, the history teacher in me appreciated, because I trust an old thing that's lasted longer than I trust a new thing that's loud.

And inside amla there's a thing it does, it helps switch on something in your body called AMPK. Teresa called it the body's energy switch. And when that switch is on, it tells your mitochondria, your power plants, to get back to work and make energy more efficiently, closer to the way they did when you were younger.

So the fuel starts flowing again. Back into your cells.

And because your nerve cells are the hungriest, the ones that felt the shortage first, they can be among the first to feel it when the fuel comes back. When those nerve cells are better supported, they can get back to the work of keeping up their protective coating and carrying their signals clean, and that burning, that buzzing, it can start to settle down so the feeling comes back instead of the noise.

Teresa also said amla's got one of the highest antioxidant loads of any food anybody's ever measured, and that part matters because antioxidants help protect those little power plants from the wear that ran them down in the first place. So you're not just refueling. You're protecting.

She told me the brand she used. Auniva. Their Amla. Two little capsules a day, made right here in the USA, and she'd been taking it for the better part of a year.

I'm going to tell you the truth about what I did next, which is I argued with myself for two more days.

The skeptic in me said: Diane, you fall for this, you're exactly the kind of person you warn your students about. The desperate widow buying magic beans.

But the other part of me, the part that had stood silent in front of 31 children, said: you have tried being a skeptic about your own feet for two years and being a skeptic hasn't given you a single night of sleep back.

And then there was the thing Teresa mentioned almost in passing. She said Auniva gives you 90 days. Take it, see what happens, and if nothing does, you send it back and they refund you. The whole thing.

And that was what tipped it. Because a skeptic's whole worry is getting taken. Getting fooled. Spending money on nothing. And here was a thing telling me, try it for three months, watch your own body, and if I was right to be skeptical, I lose nothing but the wondering.

The skeptic didn't have an argument for that. So I ordered it.

Now here's the honest account of what happened, and I'm telling it careful because I was a careful person about this the whole way through, watching myself like I'd watch a kid I suspected was exaggerating.

The first two weeks, nothing. I'll be straight with you. I almost decided it was the nonsense I'd feared.

Around week three, the nights changed first. I wasn't waking up at 2 with my feet on fire as much. I noticed because I started sleeping until the alarm, and I hadn't done that in a long, long time. I figured it was a fluke. It kept happening.

By the end of the first month the buzzing in my feet during the day had backed off. Not gone. But quieter. I'd be standing at a chalkboard and realize I wasn't thinking about my feet, which, if you've had it, you know how loud that quiet is.

And the fog. This is the one I almost can't talk about without getting emotional. Somewhere in the second month I was teaching, an actual lesson, off the top of my head, and I got to the end of a long explanation and realized I hadn't reached for a single note. The sentence had a beginning and a middle and an end and I'd walked the whole length of it without the floor dropping out.

I had to turn around and face the chalkboard for a second so the kids wouldn't see my face.

By month three I'd stopped writing out the word for word scripts. I went back to a cup of coffee and a couple bullet points, the way I'd taught my whole life. A school called me at 6:15 one morning for a long term assignment, six weeks covering a maternity leave, eighth grade history, my old subject, and I said yes without the fear that used to come with yes.

I want to be careful about what I'm claiming here, because I respect you too much to oversell it. I'm not telling you a berry rebuilt my brain. I'm telling you that the thing I'd been losing, the feeling in my feet and the sharpness in my head and the simple confidence to stand in front of a room and be myself, came back enough that I'm a working teacher again instead of a scared woman in a driveway.

That's the felt truth of it. That's what I've got.

I called Rosa and I cried again, but a different kind that time. And then I called Teresa, and I think I embarrassed her with how much I thanked her.

So here's why I'm sitting here typing this out instead of just keeping it to myself.

Because I know there's a version of you reading this who's got the buzzing in the feet. Or the fog you haven't told anybody about because you're scared of what it means. Or both, and you haven't connected them, because nobody's told you they're two ends of the same starving thing.

And I know somebody's told you it's just your age. Just your shoes. Just stress. Just one of those things.

I heard all of that. For two years. And all it did was let it get worse while I waited.

I'm not telling you to skip your doctor. Go. Keep going. I went. But I am telling you that there's a part of this nobody walked me through until a stranger on the phone did, and it's the part that finally explained why nothing I'd tried touched it. The power plants. The fuel. The hungry nerves at the end of the line.

Auniva's Amla is what helped me feed them. A little berry people have trusted for thousands of years, two capsules a day, made right here.

And you get the 90 days. That's the part I keep coming back to, because it's the part that let a lifelong skeptic finally just try. You take it, you watch your own body the way I watched mine, and if I'm wrong and it does nothing for you, you send it back and you get every dollar back. The only thing you're risking is staying right where you are, waiting, the way I waited.

I almost lost the last room in my life where I knew who I was.

I'm standing in it again Monday morning. Eighth grade history. No script. Just coffee.

If you've been standing silent in your own version of that classroom, wondering if it's all slipping away, maybe go find out why before you let anybody tell you it's just your age.

Because I'd finally said the scary thing out loud to myself. I am losing it. Whatever it is, it's winning, and nobody can tell me why, and I'm going to end up one of those people who can't be left in charge of a classroom or a checkbook or a stove.

That's where I was. I want you to know exactly how low that was, because what happened next only matters if you understand the hole I was in.

What happened next was my sister-in-law, Rosa.

Rosa was married to Frank's brother. After Frank died we stayed close, two women who'd married into the same family and outlived the men. She'd come over on Sundays. And one Sunday in the spring she's sitting at my kitchen table and I'm trying to tell her a story and I lose the word again, right in front of her, the word just gone, and I see her watching me.

And she doesn't say "are you okay" the way the kids did. She says, very quietly, "Diane. How long has that been happening?"

And I don't know why, but I told her. All of it. The feet. The burning at night. The fog. The notes I had to write now. The day I went silent in front of 31 children. I told her the scary thing, that I thought I was losing my mind, and I cried again right there at the table.

Rosa let me finish. And then she said something I wasn't expecting.

She said, "My cousin Teresa had the feet thing. The burning. The numb toes. Hers got bad, she was dropping things, couldn't feel the gas pedal right. And the fog too, she used to call it walking around in pudding."

I said, what happened to her.

And Rosa said, "She's better. She's a lot better. And it wasn't a drug. It was a little berry thing she found. I'll text her, you should talk to her."

Now I want to be honest about where my head went, because I think it's the same place yours would go.

A berry. I'm a history teacher. I deal in evidence. I have spent my whole life teaching kids the difference between what's true and what somebody wishes were true. And here's Rosa telling me her cousin fixed her numb feet and her foggy head with a piece of fruit.

I didn't believe it. Not for a second. I thought, that poor woman probably got better on her own and gave the credit to a vitamin, and now Rosa's going to have me chasing some online nonsense while my brain rots.

But I was also desperate. And desperate and skeptical can live in the same person at the same time, I've learned. So when Teresa called me that week, I picked up. And I figured I'd hear her out and then go back to being scared.

Teresa didn't try to sell me anything. That's the first thing that got me. She just told me her story, which sounded so much like mine I got goosebumps, and then she explained how the thing actually worked. And it was the explanation that turned me, not the testimonial. Because for the first time, somebody connected my feet and my fog into one single thing, and once she did, I couldn't unsee it.

Here's what she told me.

She said, think about what your nerves actually are. They're cells. And cells need energy to do their job, the same way your car needs gas. The energy in your cells gets made by these tiny little engines inside them called mitochondria. Every cell's got them. They're the power plant.

And here's the part I never knew.

Nerve cells, Teresa said, are some of the hungriest cells in your entire body. They burn through more energy than almost anything else you've got, because they're firing signals constantly, maintaining their coating, keeping the lines open. They run hot. They need a lot of fuel.

So when the power plants start running down, when your mitochondria aren't making energy the way they used to because of age and stress and processed food and all the wear of a long life, guess which cells feel it first?

The hungriest ones. The nerves.

And I just sat there on the phone in my kitchen with my hand over my mouth.

Because she'd just explained my feet and my fog in one breath. The nerves in my feet, starved for energy, sending up that tingling and burning to say something's wrong down here. And the nerves in my brain, also starved, also among the hungriest cells I've got, sitting there in the fog because they didn't have the fuel to fire clean and quick the way they used to.

Same problem. Two ends of the same body. One cause.

And every single thing my doctor had told me suddenly made sense as a thing that wouldn't work. Better shoes don't feed a starving cell. There was no pill anybody offered me, but Teresa said even the stuff people take for the burning, it just quiets the signal, it doesn't do a thing about why the signal's there. It's like the engine light's on in your car and somebody puts a piece of tape over the light. You can't see it anymore. The engine's still starving.

Nobody was feeding the power plants. That was the whole thing. That was the hole in everything I'd tried.

So then I asked the obvious question. Okay. How does a berry feed a power plant?

And this is where she told me about amla.

Amla's an Indian gooseberry. People over there have eaten it for thousands of years, which, the history teacher in me appreciated, because I trust an old thing that's lasted longer than I trust a new thing that's loud.

And inside amla there's a thing it does, it helps switch on something in your body called AMPK. Teresa called it the body's energy switch. And when that switch is on, it tells your mitochondria, your power plants, to get back to work and make energy more efficiently, closer to the way they did when you were younger.

So the fuel starts flowing again. Back into your cells.

And because your nerve cells are the hungriest, the ones that felt the shortage first, they can be among the first to feel it when the fuel comes back. When those nerve cells are better supported, they can get back to the work of keeping up their protective coating and carrying their signals clean, and that burning, that buzzing, it can start to settle down so the feeling comes back instead of the noise.

Teresa also said amla's got one of the highest antioxidant loads of any food anybody's ever measured, and that part matters because antioxidants help protect those little power plants from the wear that ran them down in the first place. So you're not just refueling. You're protecting.

She told me the brand she used. Auniva. Their Amla. Two little capsules a day, made right here in the USA, and she'd been taking it for the better part of a year.

I'm going to tell you the truth about what I did next, which is I argued with myself for two more days.

The skeptic in me said: Diane, you fall for this, you're exactly the kind of person you warn your students about. The desperate widow buying magic beans.

But the other part of me, the part that had stood silent in front of 31 children, said: you have tried being a skeptic about your own feet for two years and being a skeptic hasn't given you a single night of sleep back.

And then there was the thing Teresa mentioned almost in passing. She said Auniva gives you 90 days. Take it, see what happens, and if nothing does, you send it back and they refund you. The whole thing.

And that was what tipped it. Because a skeptic's whole worry is getting taken. Getting fooled. Spending money on nothing. And here was a thing telling me, try it for three months, watch your own body, and if I was right to be skeptical, I lose nothing but the wondering.

The skeptic didn't have an argument for that. So I ordered it.

Now here's the honest account of what happened, and I'm telling it careful because I was a careful person about this the whole way through, watching myself like I'd watch a kid I suspected was exaggerating.

The first two weeks, nothing. I'll be straight with you. I almost decided it was the nonsense I'd feared.

Around week three, the nights changed first. I wasn't waking up at 2 with my feet on fire as much. I noticed because I started sleeping until the alarm, and I hadn't done that in a long, long time. I figured it was a fluke. It kept happening.

By the end of the first month the buzzing in my feet during the day had backed off. Not gone. But quieter. I'd be standing at a chalkboard and realize I wasn't thinking about my feet, which, if you've had it, you know how loud that quiet is.

And the fog. This is the one I almost can't talk about without getting emotional. Somewhere in the second month I was teaching, an actual lesson, off the top of my head, and I got to the end of a long explanation and realized I hadn't reached for a single note. The sentence had a beginning and a middle and an end and I'd walked the whole length of it without the floor dropping out.

I had to turn around and face the chalkboard for a second so the kids wouldn't see my face.

By month three I'd stopped writing out the word for word scripts. I went back to a cup of coffee and a couple bullet points, the way I'd taught my whole life. A school called me at 6:15 one morning for a long term assignment, six weeks covering a maternity leave, eighth grade history, my old subject, and I said yes without the fear that used to come with yes.

I want to be careful about what I'm claiming here, because I respect you too much to oversell it. I'm not telling you a berry rebuilt my brain. I'm telling you that the thing I'd been losing, the feeling in my feet and the sharpness in my head and the simple confidence to stand in front of a room and be myself, came back enough that I'm a working teacher again instead of a scared woman in a driveway.

That's the felt truth of it. That's what I've got.

I called Rosa and I cried again, but a different kind that time. And then I called Teresa, and I think I embarrassed her with how much I thanked her.

So here's why I'm sitting here typing this out instead of just keeping it to myself.

Because I know there's a version of you reading this who's got the buzzing in the feet. Or the fog you haven't told anybody about because you're scared of what it means. Or both, and you haven't connected them, because nobody's told you they're two ends of the same starving thing.

And I know somebody's told you it's just your age. Just your shoes. Just stress. Just one of those things.

I heard all of that. For two years. And all it did was let it get worse while I waited.

I'm not telling you to skip your doctor. Go. Keep going. I went. But I am telling you that there's a part of this nobody walked me through until a stranger on the phone did, and it's the part that finally explained why nothing I'd tried touched it. The power plants. The fuel. The hungry nerves at the end of the line.

Auniva's Amla is what helped me feed them. A little berry people have trusted for thousands of years, two capsules a day, made right here.

And you get the 90 days. That's the part I keep coming back to, because it's the part that let a lifelong skeptic finally just try. You take it, you watch your own body the way I watched mine, and if I'm wrong and it does nothing for you, you send it back and you get every dollar back. The only thing you're risking is staying right where you are, waiting, the way I waited.

I almost lost the last room in my life where I knew who I was.

I'm standing in it again Monday morning. Eighth grade history. No script. Just coffee.

If you've been standing silent in your own version of that classroom, wondering if it's all slipping away, maybe go find out why before you let anybody tell you it's just your age.
